p: The backend implements a centralized error handling middleware as the last middleware in the Express stack. This middleware catches all errors passed via next(err) from route handlers and asynchronous operations. It distinguishes between operational errors with specific HTTP status codes and unexpected programming errors that default to 500 Internal Server Error responses.

Validation errors from Mongoose are parsed into a consistent error format with field-level messages. Each error includes the field name that failed validation and a human-readable message describing the validation requirement. The frontend uses this structured error data to display inline validation messages next to the relevant form fields, providing immediate feedback to users.

Custom error classes extend the native Error object with additional properties including status code, error code, and optional field-level details. The ApiError class accepts a status code, message, and optional errors array for validation failures. This class hierarchy enables precise error categorization and consistent error response formatting across all API endpoints.

The frontend uses a centralized Axios response interceptor to handle API errors globally. The interceptor checks the response status code and takes appropriate action for each error type. 401 Unauthorized responses trigger automatic logout and redirect to the login page. 403 Forbidden responses show an access denied notification. 409 Conflict responses display duplicate resource warnings.

Network errors and server unavailability are handled through the Axios error interceptor with a user-friendly error message displayed through a toast notification system. The application gracefully degrades when the backend is unreachable, showing cached data where available and clear error states for components that require backend connectivity.

React error boundaries catch rendering errors in component trees to prevent the entire application from crashing. Each major section of the application has its own error boundary that displays a fallback UI when an error occurs. The error details are logged to the console for development debugging while showing a friendly message to end users.

Application logging uses console.log statements in development mode and structured logging in production. Log levels include info for normal operations, warn for unexpected but handled conditions, and error for exceptions requiring investigation. Request logging captures HTTP method, URL, status code, and processing time for each API request.

The NODE_ENV environment variable controls logging verbosity and error detail exposure. In development mode, full error stack traces are returned in API responses and logged to the console. In production mode, error details are sanitized from responses while being logged server-side for security and debugging purposes.

Recommended production monitoring includes Sentry for real-time error tracking with source map support for debugging minified code. Log aggregation through services like Logtail or Papertrail centralizes logs from multiple server instances. Uptime monitoring ensures service availability with alert notifications for downtime detection.

API testing follows a layered approach with unit tests for individual controller functions, integration tests for complete request-response cycles, and end-to-end tests for multi-step user workflows. Unit tests verify business logic in isolation by mocking database operations and testing controller behavior with known inputs and expected outputs.

Integration tests use a test MongoDB database that is created and destroyed for each test suite. Supertest is the recommended library for HTTP integration testing, providing a simple API for making requests and asserting responses. Test fixtures provide consistent test data across test runs for reproducible test results.

Test coverage targets include all API endpoints with success and error scenarios. Error scenario testing covers validation failures, authentication errors, authorization denials, not found conditions, and server errors. Coverage reports identify untested code paths and guide test development priorities.

API documentation is available in two formats: the hand-written technical documentation in this document and auto-generated documentation through API documentation tools. The recommended tool for auto-generated documentation is Swagger UI with the swagger-jsdoc package that generates OpenAPI specifications from JSDoc comments in route files.

JSDoc comments in route handler files define endpoint metadata including HTTP method, URL path, request parameters, request body schema, and response format. These comments are parsed by swagger-jsdoc to generate a complete OpenAPI specification file that can be served through Swagger UI for interactive API exploration and testing.

Postman collections provide an alternative documentation format with pre-configured API requests for all endpoints. The Postman collection includes environment variables for base URL and authentication token, enabling developers to quickly test endpoints without manual configuration. Collection export files are maintained in the project repository for team collaboration.

The recommended CI/CD pipeline runs automated tests on every pull request and push to the main branch. The test pipeline installs dependencies, lints the codebase, runs unit tests, runs integration tests, and reports coverage metrics. Test failures prevent merge and deployment, ensuring only verified code reaches production.

Pre-commit hooks using Husky run linting and formatting checks before each commit. This prevents code style violations from entering the repository and ensures consistent code formatting across all contributions. The hooks run ESLint for JavaScript linting and Prettier for code formatting automatically before commit creation.

Test reporting integrates with GitHub Actions to display test results, coverage reports, and linting violations directly in pull request reviews. Coverage thresholds enforce minimum code coverage percentages for new code. Failing the coverage threshold blocks the pull request from merging, maintaining code quality standards.

The application uses environment variables for all configuration that varies between environments. The .env file in the project root stores local development configuration. The .env.example file documents all required environment variables with placeholder values for new developer onboarding. Production environments use the hosting platform's environment variable management interface.

Required environment variables include NODE_ENV for environment detection, PORT for server port configuration, MONGODB_URI for database connection string, JWT_SECRET for token signing, and FRONTEND_URL for CORS configuration. Optional variables include email service credentials, file upload size limits, and logging configuration.

Frontend environment variables prefixed with VITE_ are embedded at build time and accessible through import.meta.env. These variables include the backend API URL (VITE_API_URL) and any feature flags. Build-time embedding ensures environment-specific configuration without runtime API calls for configuration data.

Configuration validation at application startup checks that all required environment variables are set. Missing required variables cause the application to log a descriptive error message and exit immediately, preventing runtime failures due to missing configuration. This fail-fast approach simplifies debugging by catching configuration issues at startup rather than during request handling.

Environment-specific configuration files in a config directory provide default values that environment variables override. The configuration module exports a frozen configuration object that prevents runtime modification. This pattern ensures consistent configuration throughout the application lifecycle and prevents accidental configuration changes during request processing.

Secret management follows security best practices with secrets never committed to version control. The .env file is listed in .gitignore to prevent accidental commits. Production secrets use the hosting platform's secret management service or environment variable encryption. Database credentials use MongoDB Atlas connection strings with IP whitelisting for additional security.

The frontend build process uses Vite with the React plugin for optimized production bundles. The build command generates a dist folder containing minified and tree-shaken JavaScript, optimized CSS, and hashed asset filenames for cache busting. The build process runs ESLint for code quality verification before generating the production bundle.

Code splitting through React.lazy creates separate chunks for each route, reducing the initial bundle size. Chunk names are based on route component names for meaningful cache keys. Vendor chunks separate third-party dependencies from application code, enabling independent caching of stable vendor libraries and frequently updated application code.

Asset optimization includes SVG optimization, image compression, and CSS minification. The Vite build pipeline processes assets through loaders that optimize file sizes without quality loss. Source maps are generated in production for error debugging but are not deployed to production servers.

The backend requires no build step for development, running directly with Node.js from the source files. For production deployment, the backend can optionally use a build step that transpiles ES modules to CommonJS if needed. The PM2 process manager is recommended for production Node.js process management with automatic restart on failure.

Production backend configuration disables debug logging and verbose error messages. The compression middleware is enabled for optimized bandwidth. MongoDB connection pool size is increased for production workloads. Rate limiting is configured to prevent API abuse. These production optimizations are enabled automatically based on the NODE_ENV environment variable.

Dependency installation in production uses npm ci for deterministic installs based on the package-lock.json file. Dev dependencies are excluded from the production install to minimize disk usage and attack surface. The production deployment runs npm install with the --production flag to install only production dependencies.

The recommended deployment architecture uses separate hosting for the frontend and backend. The frontend static files are deployed to Vercel or Netlify for global CDN distribution with automatic SSL. The backend API is deployed to Render, Railway, or a virtual private server with reverse proxy configuration using Nginx for production traffic management.

MongoDB Atlas provides the managed database layer with automatic failover, daily backups, and point-in-time recovery. The database connection string uses the SRV format for automatic replica set discovery. IP whitelisting restricts database access to the backend server IP addresses, preventing direct database access from unauthorized locations.

Environment variables are configured through the hosting platform's dashboard or CLI tools. All secrets including JWT_SECRET, database connection strings, and third-party API keys are stored as environment variables and never hardcoded in the source code or configuration files.
